title: The yearly census numbers are out. Small places are still waiting.
dek: Since June, the Census Bureau may no longer add statistical noise to protect privacy. Its yearly survey numbers for larger places came out October 29 with slightly more tables than the old rules allowed; the five-year file that small counties and neighborhoods rely on has no date and no announced method.
author: Drafted by Claude for Robbie King
caption: Share of workers who usually work from home, by county (ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates). Every one of these 3,144 county numbers comes from the 5-year survey release, the one that now has no date.
method: Every Mapwich number was computed from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey 2020–2024 5-year estimates, as Mapwich publishes them (estimates, margins of error and population counts), with a script kept beside this piece (`numbers.mjs`). The 50 states and DC; Puerto Rico is left out. County size is the ACS 2020–2024 total population (table B01001). The Census Bureau decides which areas get 1-year estimates from its own population estimates, so the county counts against the 65,000 and 20,000 lines are close, not exact. Reliability grades follow Mapwich's rule: coefficient of variation (CV) = (margin ÷ 1.645) ÷ estimate; under 15% reliable, 15–30% use with caution, over 30% unreliable; a zero is graded unreliable when its margin is over 5 points. Outside sources are linked in the text. This piece was drafted by Claude, an AI model, for Robbie King, and reviewed by Robbie King.

body.html:
Guess first. Three questions before you read. The answers are in the piece, from Mapwich's own data.

  1. The Census Bureau's standard yearly (1-year) survey estimates cover only places of 65,000 people or more. About what share of the 3,144 U.S. counties fall below that line? A quarter, half, or three-quarters?
  2. Mapwich maps the share of workers who work from home for 83,459 census tracts. In how many is the margin of error bigger than the estimate itself?
  3. In counties of under 5,000 people, what share of work-from-home estimates does Mapwich grade unreliable, its lowest grade? And in counties of 65,000 or more?

What changed

On June 4, 2026, the Commerce Department, which runs the Census Bureau, put an order into effect called DAO 216-26, Disclosure Avoidance for Statistical Products. It says noise infusion "shall not be used for any statistical product" of the Census Bureau or the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Noise infusion means making small, deliberate changes to published numbers or to the records behind them, so that no one can pick a real person out of a table. NPR called it one of the main privacy techniques the Bureau "has used for decades." The 2020 Census used a version called differential privacy. Census Bureau leaders said in August that swapping, an older method that trades some households' details between areas, counts as noise under the order too.

The Bureau says its reading of the confidentiality law, Title 13, hasn't changed. What changed is the set of tools it may use to keep answers confidential. The order allows two methods: coarsening, publishing less detail through rounding, grouping or ranges, and suppression, withholding a number, "only as a last resort."

A Commerce spokesperson told NPR the order favors coarsening to "maintain public confidence in our data" while protecting respondents' privacy.

A late release, and one with no date

The American Community Survey (ACS) is the Census Bureau's ongoing survey of how Americans live: income, commutes, rent, health insurance, language and more. Its yearly 1-year estimates normally come out in September. This year, on August 4, the Bureau said the release date was "being determined" while it sought "DAO-compliant solutions." On October 13 it set October 29, and the 2025 1-year estimates came out that day.

For those yearly tables, the Bureau stopped swapping. It said the population floors, 65,000 people (20,000 for the supplemental tables), already give them strong protection. It also dropped three older release rules that held some tables back, so the release had nearly 38,000 more detailed tables than the old rules would have allowed, a 0.4% increase. Swapping, the same note says, was designed to protect small areas such as tracts and block groups in the 5-year products. The note doesn't say what the 5-year file will use instead.

The 5-year estimates, for 2021–2025, usually follow in December. They have no date: the Bureau's schedule says only that "release dates for the remaining 2025 ACS products will be forthcoming." The new methods will be phased into the 5-year files, with the Bureau aiming for a full transition by 2029.

That date matters most for small places, because the 5-year file is often all they get. Answer 1: three-quarters. By Mapwich's population figures, 2,308 of the 3,144 counties, 73%, have fewer than 65,000 people, so they get no standard 1-year estimates at all. Of those, 1,323 counties, 42% of all counties, are under 20,000 people, too small even for the Bureau's shorter 1-year supplemental tables. About 12.7 million people live in them. Below the county, every census tract and block group number comes only from the 5-year file.

Already at the edge

Mapwich shows the margin of error that comes with every ACS number. That margin measures sampling error: the survey asks a sample of homes, not everyone, so luck plays a part in who answered. It doesn't include the privacy noise, which was a separate, deliberate change. (Our explainer covers how to read the margins.)

The margins show how thin neighborhood numbers already are. Answer 2: 8,659 tracts, 10%. In that many of 83,459 tracts, the work-from-home margin is bigger than the estimate. Mapwich grades 41,072 of them, 49%, unreliable: hatched on the map when you turn on Hatch unreliable estimates.

Tract estimates, 50 states and DC Tracts Reliable Unreliable Margin bigger than the estimate
Workers who work from home 83,459 8% 49% 10%
Households with limited English 83,359 0.4% 65% 71%
Households with no vehicle 83,359 3% 79% 33%
No health insurance 83,466 3% 61% 11%
Population below poverty 83,418 3% 60% 5%
Households that rent 83,359 36% 21% 2%
People with a disability 83,466 20% 8% 1%

ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates as Mapwich publishes them. Grades use Mapwich's rule (see "How this was made"). The rest of each row is "use with caution" or a zero with a small margin.

Planners use these numbers anyway, and they're right to. A wide range still says something, and the ACS is often the only neighborhood source there is. The range is the honest part.

body.caption: Omaha and Douglas County, Nebraska, by tract. In Douglas County, 16.1% of workers work from home, give or take 0.6 point. Across its 163 tracts the typical margin is 5.7 points, and Mapwich grades 58 tract estimates unreliable.

body.html:
Small places first

The yearly tables cover only places of 20,000 people or more. For the 5-year file, which numbers get coarsened or withheld isn't public yet. The Bureau has said these methods can cut detail for small areas and small groups, "the places where confidentiality risks are highest." A Georgetown demographer told NPR, "There are some counties that are only a couple hundred people." North Carolina's state data center warned that rural and tribal communities are hit hardest when data are pooled into bigger areas.

Mapwich's margins show the same places are already the least certain. Answer 3: 42%, against none of the 836 counties of 65,000 or more.

County population Counties Work from home: reliable Work from home: unreliable Typical margin
Under 5,000 319 4% 42% ±4.1 points
5,000 to 19,999 1,004 19% 19% ±2.4 points
20,000 to 64,999 985 63% 2% ±1.7 points
65,000 to 249,999 549 99% 0% ±1.1 points
250,000 or more 287 100% 0% ±0.7 points

All 3,144 counties have a work-from-home estimate, ACS 2020–2024. "Typical" is the median.

body.caption: The Nebraska Sandhills, by county. Arthur, Grant, Hooker, Logan, McPherson and Blaine counties together hold 3,427 people. In Blaine County (422 people), 21.7% of workers work from home, likely anywhere from 11.5% to 31.8%.

body.html:
Texas has 52 counties under 5,000 people; Kansas and Nebraska have 38 each; North and South Dakota, 30 each. For places this small, coarsening could mean a county's number is folded into a bigger area, and suppression means a blank.

Why open methods matter

Mapwich's position is simple: data about the public should be collected openly, published as fully as privacy allows, and come with plain notes on how sure it is and how it was protected.

A range, even a wide one, is information. A planner can see that a tract's work-from-home share is "likely between 7% and 49%" and decide what to do with it: pool tracts, wait, or look for other evidence. A blank cell gives them nothing to weigh, and a number folded into a bigger area can't be split back out.

Openness about the method matters too. For the 2010 Census, the Bureau wrote in 2019, it had never publicly stated "how many households were swapped, or even the details of the algorithm." Moving to differential privacy, it promised "dramatically improved transparency" and released the source code of its 2018 test system. Coarsening and suppression are visible in their own way: you can see a blank. What users need is the rule behind each one.

What would help planners, whatever methods the Bureau uses:

  • A date for the 2021–2025 5-year estimates.
  • The rules in public: which tables and areas were coarsened or withheld, and why.
  • Margins of error kept on every number that is published.
  • Tract and block-group tables kept wherever privacy allows, rather than dropped wholesale.

What Mapwich shows meanwhile

Every ACS map on Mapwich is from the 2020–2024 5-year estimates. Click a tract or county to see its margin; turn on Hatch unreliable estimates to see which tract numbers are thin. When the 2021–2025 file arrives, we'll note what changed in how it was protected.

title: 109 bike commuters, give or take 110: how to read a neighborhood survey number
dek: Neighborhood numbers from the American Community Survey often come with very wide ranges. What they mean, why they get so wide, and how to use the numbers anyway, using bike commuting in Hennepin County, Minnesota.
author: Drafted by Claude for Robbie King
caption: Share of workers 16 and over who usually bike to work, by census tract, Hennepin County, Minnesota (ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates).
method: Every number was computed from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey 2020–2024 5-year estimates with a script kept in the repository (`apps/web/scripts/specials-numbers/acs-explainer.mjs`). It reads the Bureau's public [table-based summary files](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/) (no API key): table B08301, Means of Transportation to Work (workers 16 and over); B98001, Unweighted Housing Unit Sample; B98021, Housing Unit Response Rates; and B25001, Housing Units. Geographies: Hennepin County's 329 census tracts (2020 boundaries) and their block groups, Minneapolis city, Hennepin County and Minnesota. The script checks every Hennepin tract's bike and drive-alone shares, and the example block groups, county and state, against the values Mapwich publishes; they match. Percentage margins use the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion. Reliability grades follow Mapwich's rule: coefficient of variation (CV) = (margin ÷ 1.645) ÷ estimate; under 15% reliable, 15–30% use with caution, over 30% unreliable; a zero is graded unreliable only when its margin is over 5 points. Outside sources: Census Bureau, [ACS sample size](https://www.census.gov/acs/www/methodology/sample-size-and-data-quality/sample-size/); [*Understanding and Using American Community Survey Data: What All Data Users Need to Know*](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/library/handbooks/general.html) (2018), chapters [7](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2018/acs/acs_general_handbook_2018_ch07.pdf) and [8](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2018/acs/acs_general_handbook_2018_ch08.pdf); [*Multiyear Accuracy of the Data (5-year 2020–2024)*](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/accuracy/MultiyearACSAccuracyofData2024.pdf); [user note on 2020 margins](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/user-notes/2022-04.html); [Summary File training transcript](https://census.gov/content/dam/Census/programs-surveys/acs/guidance/training-presentations/2017_SummaryFile_Transcript_01.pdf) (2017); [SAIPE](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/saipe/about.html). ONS, [*Income estimates for small areas, England and Wales*](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/personalandhouseholdfinances/incomeandwealth/bulletins/smallareamodelbasedincomeestimates/latest) (December 2025) and [technical report](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/personalandhouseholdfinances/incomeandwealth/methodologies/incomeestimatesforsmallareasinenglandandwalestechnicalreportfinancialyearending2023). CDC, [PLACES methodology](https://www.cdc.gov/places/methodology/index.html) and [FAQ](https://www.cdc.gov/places/faqs/index.html). Statistics Canada, survey quality indicators (see note in the text). This piece was drafted by Claude, an AI model, and reviewed by Robbie King before publication.

body.html:
In one census tract just south of downtown Minneapolis, the Census Bureau estimates that 109 workers usually bike to work. The margin of error is 110. Taken at its word, the true number is somewhere between 0 and 219.

A margin bigger than the number itself looks like a broken statistic. It isn't. It's an honest statement of how little a survey can say about one small neighborhood, and the same survey, read the right way, is still the best source there is. Here is why, using the 329 census tracts of Hennepin County, Minnesota.

One home in 41

The American Community Survey (ACS) is the Census Bureau's ongoing survey of how Americans live: jobs, commutes, rent, income, health insurance, internet access and more. Unlike the census every ten years, it doesn't ask everyone. In 2024 it picked 3,543,672 addresses, about one home in 41, from the Bureau's master list of addresses. Small places are sampled at higher rates and big, populous tracts at lower ones.

A single year is far too few answers for a neighborhood, so for small areas the Bureau pools five years. The newest set covers 2020 through 2024. Over those five years, 56,099 Hennepin County addresses were picked, about one home in 10, and 36,133 households completed the survey, about one home in 16. Spread across the county's 329 tracts, that is about 110 completed surveys per tract, on average.

What the ± means

Every ACS number comes with a margin of error, published at 90% confidence. In the Bureau's words, it gives a range "expected to contain the true or population value of an estimate 90 percent of the time." So "109 ± 110" means the true count is most likely between 0 and 219. A count can't be negative, so the low end stops at zero.

The margin only covers the luck of the draw: which homes happened to be picked. It doesn't cover questions misread or left blank, so the Bureau says its error measures are "only lower bounds of the total error."

Why small places get wide ranges

Two things make a range wide: few answers, and an uncommon answer. Bike commuting is uncommon: 0.89% of Hennepin's workers do it. In a tract, the survey may reach only a handful of households with a bike commuter, and each answer stands in for many homes; Hennepin has about 16 homes for every completed survey. Whether the survey happened to reach three of those households or six changes the estimate a lot, and the margin says so.

So a margin bigger than the estimate doesn't mean the survey talked to fewer people than the margin. It means the sample can say "some," but not how many.

Zeros work the same way. In 170 Hennepin tracts the estimate is zero bike commuters, with margins of 10, 14 or 16. The survey found none among the homes it reached; the margin, worked out by a special method for zeros, says there could still be a few.

In all, 278 of the 329 tracts have a bike-commuter margin larger than the estimate. Only one count passes the usual reliability test: tract 1040.01 in Southeast Minneapolis, 122 ± 28, likely between 94 and 150. Even there, the share of workers who bike only rates "use with caution," because the number of workers is an estimate too.

body.caption: Central Minneapolis, by tract. Tract 59.02, just south of downtown: 7.7% of workers bike, likely between 0.1% and 15.4%. Tract 1040.01, east of the river: 6.0%, likely between 4.0% and 7.9%. Similar estimates, very different certainty.

body.html:
The trouble is the uncommon answer, not the place. Ask the same tracts how many people drive to work alone, the most common answer, and the picture flips.

Share of workers who… Reliable (CV under 15%) Use with caution (15–30%) Unreliable (over 30%, hatched) Zero, not graded
Bike to work 0 4 155 169
Work from home 96 186 46 0
Drive alone 290 34 4 0

Hennepin County's census tracts, graded as Mapwich grades them (CV is explained below); one tract has no workers. ACS 2020–2024, table B08301.

body.caption: Same area, share of workers who drive alone to work. Across Hennepin, 290 of these tract estimates are reliable; 4 are not.

body.html:
Zoom out and the range shrinks

Combine areas and the margin shrinks compared with the estimate. The table follows bike commuting from one block group, the smallest area the ACS reports, up to the state.

Area Workers 16+ Share who bike Likely between Margin as a share of the estimate
Block group 3, tract 59.02 733 11.6% 0% and 24.8% 114%
Tract 59.02 1,410 7.7% 0.1% and 15.4% 99%
Minneapolis 239,419 2.02% 1.76% and 2.27% 13%
Hennepin County 686,167 0.89% 0.80% and 0.97% 10%
Minnesota 2,939,889 0.47% 0.44% and 0.49% 6%

ACS 2020–2024, table B08301. Each row is a bigger place, not the same place seen more sharply, so the share itself changes too.

Adding areas works because their sampling errors partly cancel out. To get the margin of a sum, the Bureau says to square each margin, add them up and take the square root. Tract 59.02's three block groups estimate 0, 24 and 85 bike commuters, with margins of 10, 38 and 102. Added up, that's 109 with a margin of 109, almost exactly the 110 the Bureau publishes for the tract.

Do the same with all 329 tracts and you get the county's total, 6,080 bike commuters, with a margin of 627. The Bureau's own figure, worked out from the full survey records, is 610. The margin went from bigger than the estimate to about a tenth of it. The formula is an approximation, so when the Bureau publishes a figure for the bigger area, use that.

Why it's still worth using

  • It's often the only source. A Census Bureau trainer put it plainly: for tracts, block groups and other small areas, "the ACS is often the only source of information."
  • It's consistent. The sample is drawn from every county in the country and processed with one set of methods, so a tract in Hennepin can be set beside one anywhere else.
  • People answer. The Bureau reports a response rate of 82.7% for Hennepin County's sampled homes over 2020–2024.
  • It tells you how sure it is. Every number arrives with its own margin. Many data sources give you a number and nothing else.

Rules of thumb

  1. Read the range, not the number. "Likely between 0.1% and 15.4%" says more than "7.7%."
  2. Size up the margin against the number. If the margin is less than about a quarter of the estimate, the number is solid. Between a quarter and a half, use it with caution. More than half, treat it as a rough guide. Mapwich uses those cut-offs (statisticians call the measure behind them the coefficient of variation), though the Bureau itself says there are "no hard-and-fast rules".
  3. Combine areas when single tracts are too fuzzy, with the formula above.
  4. Test a difference; don't eyeball it. Tracts 59.02 and 1040.01 differ by 1.8 points, but the margin of that difference is 7.9 points, so the survey can't tell them apart. The Bureau warns that checking whether two ranges overlap "will not always provide an accurate result."
  5. Use the 5-year file for small areas. Single-year estimates exist only for areas of 65,000 people or more. A 5-year estimate is an average over the period, not a snapshot of its last year. Compare periods that don't overlap, such as 2015–2019 and 2020–2024. And 2020–2024 includes 2020, when the pandemic cut the survey to about two-thirds of its usual responses, so its margins run wider.
  6. Treat percentages with care. Both halves of a share are estimates: tract 59.02's 1,410 workers carry their own margin of 288.

How Mapwich shows it

Click a tract and the details panel shows the estimate with its ±. When the margin is wide, it spells out the range: for tract 59.02, "Few households were surveyed here, so this is a range: likely between 0.09% and 15%." In the legend, Hatch unreliable estimates draws light stripes over tracts and block groups with a CV over 30% (or a zero with a margin over 5 points); the color still shows. On change-over-time maps, a change smaller than its margin of error is labeled No clear change. Mapwich doesn't yet have the published margins for earlier periods, so it estimates those from the latest one.

How other surveys handle it

  • The UK doesn't lean on survey answers alone. Its statistics office estimates income for 7,264 neighborhoods in England and Wales by blending a household survey with the 2021 Census and government records. Every number still comes with a range, and the office tells you to look at those ranges any time you compare or rank places.
  • CDC PLACES, where Mapwich's health maps come from, also uses a statistical model. It takes a big national health survey and predicts what each tract probably looks like, with a range for each. Those ranges come out narrower, but the model can't see what's happening on the ground, like a new local health program, so the CDC says not to use the numbers to judge those programs.

Models narrow the range by borrowing from other data; the ACS sticks to what people in each place said, and shows the cost in the width of its ranges. Either way, the good habit is the same: say how sure you are, next to the number, in plain words.

title: America's biking capital isn't where you think
dek: No county has a larger share of workers who bike to work than Holmes County, Ohio, where it's about one in seven. The county number is solid. Many of the neighborhood numbers behind it, here and elsewhere, are not.
author: Drafted by Claude for Robbie King
caption: Share of workers 16 and over who usually biked to work, by county (ACS 2020–2024). Darker blue means a larger share. Holmes County, Ohio, has the highest estimate of the 3,222 counties. In 3,028 of them, fewer than 1% of workers bike.
method:
Every number from Mapwich data in the text was computed from Mapwich's published county and tract files with a script kept with this piece (`apps/web/scripts/specials-numbers/holmes-county-bikes.mjs`); the table of commuting shares is computed from the same files when the site is built. Margins of error are the Census Bureau's, at 90% confidence. Reliability grades follow Mapwich's rule: the coefficient of variation, (margin ÷ 1.645) ÷ estimate, under 15% is reliable, 15% to 30% "use with caution", over 30% unreliable; an estimate of zero is not graded. Earlier periods (2010–2014 and 2015–2019) have no margins of error on Mapwich, so changes over time are not tested. Approximate county populations are the 2020 Census count per square mile times land area. The distance from the University of Minnesota is measured from each tract's center point to a point on the East Bank campus (Northrop Auditorium).

Mapwich maps counties and tracts, not cities, so the figures for the City of Minneapolis are not Mapwich data. They come from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year tables, retrieved from data.census.gov on 12 October 2026: shares with margins from table S0801 ([2020–2024](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2024.S0801?g=160XX00US2743000), [2015–2019](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2019.S0801?g=160XX00US2743000)), and the counts of workers and bike commuters for Minneapolis and Holmes County from table [B08301, 2020–2024](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B08301?g=050XX00US39075,160XX00US2743000). Mapwich works out its share margins from these counts; for Holmes County that gives ±2.2 points, where table S0801 shows ±2.1. Portland's and Davis's shares and margins are worked out the same way from table B08301, 2020–2024 ([Portland](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B08301?g=160XX00US4159000), [Davis](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B08301?g=160XX00US0618100)), retrieved through [Census Reporter](https://censusreporter.org/) on 27 October 2026.

Award and rating facts: the League of American Bicyclists' [2025 Bicycle Friendly Community report card for Minneapolis](https://bikeleague.org/wp-content/uploads/bfareportcards/bfc/2025/Minneapolis_MN.pdf) (award level, history, scoring areas, the city's own bike-share estimate) and its [award database](https://bikeleague.org/bfa/award-database/) (counts of current award holders and the absence of any Holmes County community, checked 12 October 2026); PeopleForBikes' [2026 City Ratings results](https://www.peopleforbikes.org/news/2026s-best-places-to-bike) (16 June 2026) and [methodology](https://www.peopleforbikes.org/news/2026-city-ratings-methodology) (28 April 2026), and its [Minneapolis page](https://cityratings.peopleforbikes.org/cities/minneapolis-mn). Portland's and Davis's first Platinum awards are from BikePortland's reports at the time ([2005](https://bikeportland.org/2005/09/28/california-city-is-first-to-platinum-487/), [2008](https://bikeportland.org/2008/04/29/portland-gets-platinum-becomes-first-major-us-city-to-win-the-award/)). The Holmes County Trail is described by the [Holmes County Chamber of Commerce](https://www.holmescountychamber.com/recreation/holmes-county-rails-trails-coalition).

Amish settlement sizes and the counties each settlement covers are from the [Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies, Elizabethtown College](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/twelve-largest-settlements-2024/) (2024 estimates; [by county](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/files/2024/08/Amish-Pop-2024_by-state-and-county_c.pdf)). Which communities use bicycles or scooters is from Erik Wesner of Amish America, [*Do Amish people ride bicycles?*](https://amishamerica.com/do-amish-ride-bicycles/) (updated 2024) and [*Why do some Amish ride scooters (but not bicycles)?*](https://amishamerica.com/why-do-amish-ride-scooters-but-not-bicycles/) (2020, updated 2024); e-bikes in Holmes County from Kyle Barnett, [*Some Amish are embracing e-bikes*](https://mountvernonnews.com/stories/649415724-some-amish-are-embracing-e-bikes-as-a-form-of-transportation), Mount Vernon News (2023). Tract sizes are from the [Census Bureau's geography glossary](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/about/glossary.html). This piece was drafted by Claude, an AI model, from Mapwich data, and reviewed by Robbie King before publication.

body.html:
Ask people where Americans bike to work and most will name a big city or a college town. The county map says otherwise. The county with the largest share of workers who usually bike to work is Holmes County, Ohio: 14.0%, about one worker in seven, in the Census Bureau's American Community Survey for 2020–2024. Next is LaGrange County, Indiana, at 7.2%. San Francisco County is at 3.3%, the District of Columbia at 3.3%, and Multnomah County, Oregon, which includes Portland, at 2.8%.

Biking to work is rare almost everywhere. In 3,028 of the 3,222 counties, fewer than 1% of workers bike, and the typical county is at 0.09%. That is why a county of about 44,000 people stands out so sharply on the map.

How sure can we be?

The survey reaches a sample of households, so every estimate has a margin of error and gives us a range of the real value as if we were able to ask everyone. Holmes County's is ±2.2 points. With 90% confidence, the true share is between 11.8% and 16.2%, and the estimate is graded reliable. Even the low end is above the top of LaGrange County's range (7.2% ±1.2), so the county ranking holds up.

Neighborhood numbers are another matter. A census tract usually has between 1,200 and 8,000 residents, and the survey reaches only some of their households. Of the 84,378 tracts with a bike-to-work estimate, 63,956 (76%) show zero. A zero usually means the survey found no bike commuters among the households it reached, not that nobody bikes. At the other end, the highest tract estimate in the country, 47.1% for a tract on Nantucket, has a margin of ±45.1 points. It is graded unreliable.

Holmes County up close

body.caption: Holmes County, Ohio, and its neighbors, by census tract. The high shares are on the county's east side; two tracts in the west show none. Turn on reliability hatching in the full map to see which tract numbers are shaky.

body.html:
Inside the county, the numbers split east and west: three of the ten tracts are above one worker in five, all east or southeast of the center, and two in the west and southwest show zero.

Tract 9768.01, southeast of the center, is at 37.5% ±6.4, the highest tract estimate in the country that Mapwich grades reliable. Its neighbor, Tract 9768.02, is at 27.3% ±13.5: the true share could be anywhere from 13.8% to 40.8%, and it is graded unreliable. For areas this small, the county figure is the better guide.

Bicycles and scooters

Holmes County gives its name to one of the country's largest Amish settlements: 40,435 people in 2024, by the estimate of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College, reaching into Coshocton, Tuscarawas and Wayne counties. Only the Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, settlement is larger.

The census does not ask about religion, so the map cannot say who is riding. What it shows does line up with what has been written about Amish travel. Amish church communities set their own rules on technology, and they differ on bicycles. The guide Amish America lists Holmes County, northern Indiana's Shipshewana and Nappanee areas, and Arthur, Illinois, among communities where bicycles are common. It lists Lancaster County, Geauga County in Ohio, Allen County in Indiana, and Dover, Delaware, among communities that use push scooters instead. Local reporting describes electric bikes catching on in Holmes County, though not every church allows them.

Set beside the census numbers, the two lists split cleanly:

  • Bicycle communities. LaGrange County, in the third-largest settlement (Elkhart-LaGrange, 29,180 people), is second in the country at 7.2% ±1.2. Douglas County, Illinois, in the Arthur-Arcola settlement, is 16th at 4.0% ±1.3.
  • Scooter communities. Lancaster County is at 0.7% ±0.1, Geauga County at 0.1% ±0.1, and Allen County, Indiana, and Kent County, Delaware (Dover), near 0.3%.

One caution: Lancaster County has about 553,000 residents and Geauga about 95,000, so Amish workers are a much smaller share of all workers there than in Holmes. A county average shows a community's habits only where that community is a large part of the county.

Biking is not the only way these counties stand apart.

body.title: How workers get to work, and households without a car
body.caption: ACS 2020–2024. Holmes, LaGrange and Douglas counties are in settlements where bicycles are common; Lancaster and Geauga in settlements that use scooters. Hennepin County, Minnesota, includes Minneapolis.

body.html:
In Holmes and LaGrange counties, fewer than half of workers drive alone (47.8% and 47.7%), and nearly a third of households have no vehicle (30.9% and 29.2%). Holmes County also has 6.9% walking to work; with biking, that's about one worker in five.

Minneapolis, Portland and Davis, for comparison

The League of American Bicyclists has rated Minneapolis a Gold Bicycle Friendly Community since 2011, most recently in 2025, and PeopleForBikes' 2026 City Ratings put it second among large U.S. cities.

By the Census Bureau's measure, 2.0% ±0.3 of Minneapolis workers usually biked to work in 2020–2024, about 4,800 people. The city's own 2025 award application put its bike share at 2% to 5%, combining census figures, trip diaries and counts. Hennepin County, which also takes in the suburbs, is at 0.9% ±0.1.

body.caption: Minneapolis, by census tract. The higher shares cluster around the University of Minnesota, east of downtown. Same colors as the Holmes County map.

body.html:
Within the city, the higher tract numbers cluster near the University of Minnesota: the 24 tracts centered within 3 kilometers of campus have a middle value of 2.3%, while 165 of Hennepin County's 304 other tracts show zero.

The city's share has halved since 2015–2019, when it was 4.0% ±0.3, a drop far larger than the margins. Over the same years, the share working from home went from 5.8% to 26.2%, and the later survey years include the pandemic. These figures cannot say how much one change had to do with the other.

Two other cities share the top of the bike-friendly lists. Portland, Oregon, became the first large U.S. city the League rated Platinum, in 2008, and is eighth among large cities in PeopleForBikes' 2026 City Ratings. By the Census Bureau's measure, 3.4% ±0.3 of Portland workers usually biked to work in 2020–2024, about 12,000 people.

Davis, California, was the League's first Platinum community of any size, in 2005. Its share is the highest of the three cities: 11.2% ±1.5, about 3,700 workers. That range, 9.8% to 12.7%, overlaps Holmes County's (11.8% to 16.2%), so the survey can't say which is higher. Davis is a city and Holmes is a county, though: Yolo County, which takes in Davis, is at 4.9%.

body.title: Bike to work across three survey periods
body.caption: ACS 5-year estimates for 2010–2014, 2015–2019 and 2020–2024. Margins of error for the two earlier periods aren't on Mapwich, so small changes may not be real.

body.html:
Holmes County went the other way, from 8.1% to 14.0%, while its share working from home rose by less than one point; in 2015–2019 it ranked second, behind Mackinac County, Michigan. Mapwich has no margins for the earlier periods, so we can't say whether that jump is more than sampling noise. Part of the headline is a 2020s story.

Why Holmes County isn't on the bike-friendly lists

If Holmes County leads the census measure, why isn't it on lists of the best places to bike? Part of the answer is that the lists measure something else.

The League's award starts with an application from a town, city or county. Reviewers score it in five areas: engineering, education, encouragement, evaluation and planning, and equity and accessibility. Each report card also shows the share of commuters who bike, and reviewers told Minneapolis that evidence of more riding would be "critical" to reaching Platinum, the top level. The League's award database lists 447 communities, including 19 counties and 21 places listed as rural. None is in Holmes County, and we found no record of a Holmes County application.

PeopleForBikes works from map data instead. Its City Ratings score 3,019 cities on how well low-stress streets and paths inside city limits connect homes to jobs, shops, schools and other everyday places. How many people ride is not part of the score. The 2026 ratings have no page for Millersburg, the county seat, or other Holmes County villages we checked.

The census measure looks only at how workers usually get to work.

Holmes County, Ohio Minneapolis
Workers 16 and over 20,065 ±559 239,419 ±2,736
Usually biked to work 2,813 ±450 4,825 ±606
Share who biked 14.0% ±2.2 2.0% ±0.3
League award None Gold since 2011
PeopleForBikes rating, 2026 No rated place 68 out of 100

Minneapolis has about 12 times as many workers as Holmes County, but fewer than twice as many bike commuters.

The awards and ratings describe what a place has built and planned for people on bikes; the census describes how people get to work. They answer different questions. Holmes County does have the Holmes County Trail, a paved rail trail shared by bicyclists, walkers, horseback riders and buggies.

The top of the list, with margins

County estimates are steadier than tract estimates. Holmes County's lead is clear; below it, the margins overlap enough that the order could easily change.

County Bike to work (%) Margin of error (points) Grade
Holmes County, OH 14.0 ±2.2 Reliable
LaGrange County, IN 7.2 ±1.2 Reliable
Pitkin County, CO 6.7 ±2.1 Use with caution
Presidio County, TX 6.3 ±4.7 Unreliable
Grand County, UT 6.3 ±3.1 Use with caution
San Juan County, CO 5.9 ±4.2 Unreliable

Of the 69 tracts nationwide with estimates of 15% or more, 46 are graded unreliable and only 6 reliable. Five of those six are in California, within 2 kilometers of the Stanford, UC Davis and UC Santa Barbara campuses. The sixth is in Holmes County.

What the map can't tell us

The census counts how workers 16 and over usually got to work, not trips to school, the store or church. It can't say how many of Holmes County's bike commuters are Amish, and we couldn't find whether the survey tells people on electric bikes to answer "bicycle". Tract numbers rest on small samples. The county number, 14.0% ±2.2, is the solid one.

What the map does show is a small Ohio county where biking to work is about four times as common as in San Francisco, and where it goes with more walking and more households without a car.

title: Traffic death rates run highest where the fewest people live
dek: About 41,000 people a year died in U.S. traffic crashes from 2020 to 2024. Per resident, the toll is several times higher in thinly settled counties than in big cities, and serious injuries, which are far more common, have no national county map at all.
author: Drafted by Claude for Robbie King
caption: Average yearly traffic deaths per 100,000 residents, 2020–2024, by county (NHTSA FARS). Darker purple means a higher rate; each shade holds a fifth of counties, and the darkest starts at 30.7. Deaths are counted where the crash happened. Connecticut is blank because its crash records use the old county codes.
method: Every number from Mapwich data in the text was computed from Mapwich's exported state and county values with a script kept in the repository (`apps/web/scripts/specials-numbers/traffic-deaths.mjs`); the chart and table are computed from the same files when the site is built. Mapwich stores rates, not counts. Death counts in the text are rebuilt from the rates the same way the rates were made: rate × residents ÷ 100,000, with residents from the ACS 2020–2024 population (2015–2019 for years before 2020). National figures are rebuilt from state values, so they can differ by a few dozen deaths from NHTSA's published totals. Deaths per mile driven divide 2020–2024 average deaths by 2024 vehicle miles on counted roads (FHWA HPMS), which leave out some local roads, so they run higher than NHTSA's national figures. Statements that one measure "tends to" rise with another rest on Spearman rank correlations (density and death rate: −0.52 nationally, −0.59 within states, which removes each state's average rank first; miles per resident and density: −0.46; miles per resident and death rate: 0.50; share of Native residents and death rate: 0.08). Outside figures: NHTSA, [*Overview of Motor Vehicle Traffic Crashes in 2023*](https://crashstats.nhtsa.dot.gov/Api/Public/ViewPublication/813705) (DOT HS 813 705) and [*Rural/Urban Comparison of Traffic Fatalities: 2022 Data*](https://crashstats.nhtsa.dot.gov/Api/Public/ViewPublication/813599) (DOT HS 813 599); FHWA, [*National Performance Management Measures: Highway Safety Improvement Program*](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2016/03/15/2016-05202/national-performance-management-measures-highway-safety-improvement-program), 81 FR 13882 (2016); [CDC, Tribal Road Safety](https://www.cdc.gov/tribal-road-safety/about/index.html); [National Park Service, Fort Wingate Historic District](https://www.nps.gov/places/fort-wingate-historic-district.htm); U.S. Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, [*Enhancing Tribal Self-Governance and Safety of Indian Roads*](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-116shrg36243/html/CHRG-116shrg36243.htm), S. Hrg. 116-15 (2019); [University of Arizona, Native American Advancement, Initiatives and Research: Navajo Nation](https://naair.arizona.edu/navajo-nation). This piece was drafted by Claude, an AI model, from Mapwich data, and reviewed by Robbie King before publication.

body.html:
From 2020 through 2024, about 41,000 people a year died in motor vehicle crashes in the United States: 12.3 for every 100,000 residents, according to NHTSA's Fatality Analysis Reporting System. The map above shows where those crashes happened, county by county.

By state, Mississippi has the highest rate, 25.1 deaths per 100,000 residents a year, followed by Wyoming (21.4), Arkansas (20.9), New Mexico (20.7) and South Carolina (20.6). Massachusetts has the lowest, 5.4, with Rhode Island, New York, the District of Columbia and Hawaii close behind. Mississippi's rate is 4.7 times Massachusetts's.

A rise, then a slow fall

Deaths jumped during the pandemic. The national rate went from 11.2 per 100,000 in 2019 to 12.9 in 2021, when about 43,200 people died, the highest single year from 2014-2024. It has fallen every year since, to 11.7 in 2024, but that is still higher than any year from 2015 to 2019.

Year Traffic deaths per 100,000 residents
2015 10.9
2016 11.6
2017 11.5
2018 11.3
2019 11.2
2020 11.6
2021 12.9
2022 12.8
2023 12.2
2024 11.7

National rate for each year, from NHTSA's FARS files. 2015–2019 use the 2015–2019 ACS population; 2020–2024 use the 2020–2024 population.

Fewer people, higher rates

The clearest pattern on the map is density. Sort the 3,135 counties with a value by people per square mile and cut them into ten equal groups. In the least crowded tenth, under 4 people per square mile, the typical county's rate is 34.9. In the most crowded tenth, 427 people per square mile and up, it is 8.4, about a quarter as high.

body.title: Traffic death rates fall as counties get more crowded
body.caption: Median county traffic death rate (2020–2024 yearly average, NHTSA FARS) in each tenth of counties, sorted by people per square mile (ACS 2020–2024). Medians, because a few tiny counties have extreme rates.

body.html:
It isn't just rural states against urban ones. Inside each state, the emptier counties still tend to have the higher death rates, and the pattern is a little stronger within states than across the country as a whole. Counties with fewer than 50 people per square mile hold 8.8% of the people but 17.3% of the deaths, a combined rate of 24.1. Counties with 500 or more hold 54.2% of the people and 39.1% of the deaths, a combined rate of 8.9.

Driving goes along with it. People in emptier counties tend to drive more, and counties with more driving per resident tend to have higher death rates. Per mile driven, though, the gap narrows but doesn't close. Dividing deaths by miles driven on counted roads gives 1.73 deaths per 100 million vehicle miles in the least crowded tenth of counties and 1.16 in the most crowded. NHTSA's own figures for 2022 show a similar gap: 1.68 deaths per 100 million miles in rural areas and 1.15 in urban ones. Rural areas held about 20% of the population and 41% of the deaths, and about two-thirds of rural deaths were in crashes where a vehicle left its lane or the road.

Counted where the crash happens

The rate on this map divides deaths where crashes happened by the people who live there. Where few people live and many drive through, the rate can soar. West Texas shows it most clearly.

body.caption: West Texas, by county. Same colors as the main map. Of the 27 Texas counties west of 101°W and south of 33°N, 23 are in the darkest shade. The four exceptions, El Paso, Midland, Ector and Val Verde, are the area's four most populous counties.

body.html:
Loving County, Texas, had 64 residents in the 2020 Census, and the ACS estimate is 33. Nineteen people died in crashes there over the five years, so its rate is 11,520 per 100,000, by far the highest in the country. Its counted roads carry 7,113 vehicle miles a day for every resident, 236 times the typical county. Hudspeth and Culberson counties, east of El Paso, had 71 deaths between them and about 5,600 residents. Their rates, 258.6 and 246.0, say as much about the traffic passing through as about the people who live there.

Small numbers matter too. In a county of 2,000 people, one more death in five years moves the yearly rate by 10. Of the 46 counties with rates above 100, 44 have fewer than 10,000 residents. And 31 counties had no traffic deaths at all from 2020 to 2024.

body.title: Seven counties, from nearly empty to very crowded
body.caption: Vehicle miles per resident: daily miles driven on counted roads in the county, per resident (FHWA HPMS 2024). Shelby County, Tennessee, home to Memphis, is a reminder that density isn't everything.

body.html:
Shelby County's rate, 26.6, is 2.2 times the national rate, the ninth-highest of the 607 counties with 100,000 or more residents. New York County (Manhattan), at 2.3, and Arlington County, Virginia, at 2.2, have the lowest.

The Four Corners

A second cluster stands out in the Southwest, and through-traffic doesn't explain it the same way.

body.caption: The Four Corners, by county. Same colors as the main map. Apache, Navajo and Coconino counties in Arizona, McKinley and Cibola in New Mexico, and San Juan County, Utah, are all in the darkest shade.

body.html:
Apache, Navajo and Coconino counties in Arizona and McKinley County in New Mexico each have rates between 36.9 and 38.6, roughly twice their states' rates (Arizona 16.5, New Mexico 20.7). Together they recorded 730 deaths in five years. Their vehicle miles per resident, 35 to 47 a day, are only modestly above the typical county's 30. Much of the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation in the United States, lies in these counties; in Apache and McKinley counties, 71% and 75% of residents are American Indian (ACS 2020–2024).

Nationally, counties with more Native residents don't consistently have higher death rates, partly because the 12 Alaska counties where Native residents are a quarter or more of the population have low rates (median 5.9). Outside Alaska, the 35 such counties have a combined rate of 37.3, about three times the national rate.

The CDC reports that American Indian and Alaska Native people have the highest motor vehicle death rates of any racial or ethnic group. The roads they travel have a history. In the 1860s the U.S. Army forced thousands of Navajo people on a 400-mile march, the Long Walk, to the Bosque Redondo Reservation in New Mexico; a treaty in 1868 let them return home. Today the Bureau of Indian Affairs runs a road system on tribal lands. At a 2019 Senate hearing, it said about 17,130 miles of those roads were unimproved earth roads, with $392 million in deferred maintenance in 2018. The Federal Highway Administration told the same hearing that "many Tribes are not adequately represented in State and national crash databases," so counts like these may be low.

Serious injuries: the map we don't have

For every traffic death there are many more serious injuries, but there is no national county map of them, and Mapwich doesn't have one. FARS, the source of the death counts, covers fatal crashes only. NHTSA estimates injuries from a sample of police crash reports: about 2.44 million people were injured in 2023, about 60 for every death. Those are national estimates, not county ones, and they count injuries of every severity.

Serious injuries are counted by the states. A 2016 federal rule requires every state transportation department to track the number of serious injuries, using a common definition taken from police crash reports, and to set targets on five-year averages. Those counts sit in each state's own crash records, and Mapwich hasn't brought them together.

What the map can't tell us

This map counts deaths where crashes happened, not where the people who died resided. It can't say who was driving, how fast, or why a crash happened, and it can't separate the road from the traffic on it. A county's rate can also swing on a handful of crashes.

What it does show is steady. Traffic deaths per resident are highest in the emptiest counties, and the gap holds within states and per mile driven. In a few places the numbers mostly reflect traffic passing through. In others, like the Navajo Nation, they fall on the people who live there.

title: Work from home, work out more? What the county map can and can't tell us
dek: Counties where more people work from home have fewer adults who skip exercise altogether. The pattern is strong and it's real, but most of it follows income and education, and part of it is built into how the health numbers are made.
author: Drafted by Claude for Robbie King
caption: Work from home (2020–2024) against adults with no leisure-time exercise (2023), by county. Blue counties have many home workers and few non-exercisers; gold counties the reverse. 2,956 counties have both values; Kentucky and Pennsylvania are blank because the inactivity data has no county values for them.
method: Every number from Mapwich data in the text was computed from Mapwich's exported county values with a script kept in the repository (`apps/web/scripts/specials-numbers/work-from-home-and-exercise.mjs`); the chart and tables are computed from the same files when the site is built. Correlations are Spearman rank correlations (ρ). "Within states" removes each state's average rank first. "Holding income and education equal" is a partial rank correlation: both measures' ranks are adjusted for the ranks of median household income and the bachelor's degree share before they are compared. Virginia's independent cities count as counties, as the Census Bureau treats them. The inactivity estimates come from a statistical model ([CDC PLACES methodology](https://www.cdc.gov/places/methodology/index.html)); the survey question is on [CDC's measure definitions page](https://www.cdc.gov/places/measure-definitions/health-risk-behaviors.html). The history of Pine Ridge and Rosebud draws on [Oglala Lakota County](https://oglalalakotacountysd.gov/about-3/), the [Bureau of Indian Affairs](https://www.bia.gov/regional-offices/great-plains/south-dakota/rosebud-agency), [*United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians*, 448 U.S. 371 (1980)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/448/371) and the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, [*Broken Promises: Continuing Federal Funding Shortfall for Native Americans*](https://www.usccr.gov/reports/2018/broken-promises-continuing-federal-funding-shortfall-native-americans) (2018). This piece was drafted by Claude, an AI model, from Mapwich data, and checked against that data before publication.

body.html:
Look at the map above and two colors do most of the talking. Blue marks counties in the top third for the share of workers who work from home and the bottom third for adults who got no exercise at all in the past month. Gold marks the opposite: few home workers, many adults with no leisure-time activity. Blue is common in the West: 43 of Colorado's 64 counties are blue, and 29 of Washington's 39. About half of the 632 blue counties have 100 or more people per square mile. Gold is concentrated in the South. In Mississippi, 67 of 82 counties are gold, and 483 of the 596 gold counties nationwide are in 14 southern states from Texas to Virginia.

Across the 2,956 counties with both numbers, the link is strong: a rank correlation of −0.62. It is not just one region of the country against another, either. Comparing counties only with others in the same state, it is still −0.53.

So does working from home get people moving? The tempting story writes itself: no commute, more time for a walk. The county data can't confirm that story, and when you look closely, most of the pattern turns out to be about something else.

How big the gap is

Sort the counties by their work-from-home share and cut them into ten equal groups of about 296 counties each. In the tenth with the fewest home workers (under 4.2% of workers), an average of 33.1% of adults report no leisure-time exercise. In the tenth with the most (16.4% and up), it's 20.8%.

body.title: Fewer adults skip exercise in counties where more people work from home
body.caption: Work from home is the share of workers 16 and over who usually worked from home (ACS 2020–2024). No leisure-time exercise is the age-adjusted share of adults who answered no to any exercise outside their job in the past month (CDC PLACES, 2023).

body.html:
That's a gap of about 12 percentage points, in a measure where the typical county sits at 26.5%. It's a big difference, but it doesn't tell us why.

Virginia, where the two line up

Virginia shows the pattern clearly. Across its 133 counties and independent cities the rank correlation is −0.72, stronger than the national figure. The close-up below runs from the Washington suburbs in the northeast to the rural counties of the southwest.

body.caption: Virginia and West Virginia, by county. Northern Virginia, at top right, is mostly blue: seven of its nine counties and independent cities. West Virginia, at left, is mostly gold, brown or dark: 47 of its 55 counties are in the top third for inactivity. Same colors as the main map.

body.html:
In Arlington County, 35.3% of workers work from home and 15.1% of adults report no leisure-time exercise. In Giles County, in the southwest, 2.5% work from home and 24.9% report no exercise. Grayson County, also in the southwest, is at 5.2% and 31.3%.

The table shows how else these counties differ.

body.title: Four counties in northern and central Virginia, four in the southwest
body.caption: Median household income and the share of adults 25 and over with a bachelor's degree are ACS 2020–2024 estimates.

body.html:
In the first four, median household incomes run from $104,400 to $181,800, and three in five adults or more have a bachelor's degree. In the four southwestern counties incomes are between $47,730 and $65,690 and fewer than one adult in five has a degree. Working from home, exercise, income and education all move together here. Any one of them could be standing in for the others.

The northern Plains, where the pattern breaks

Now move to the Dakotas and eastern Montana. Here the link mostly disappears: within South Dakota the correlation is 0.03, essentially none; in North Dakota −0.14; in Montana −0.09.

body.caption: The Dakotas and eastern Montana, by county. Much of the region is blue or pale, but five South Dakota counties are dark: in the top third for both working from home and inactivity. Same colors as the main map.

body.html:
Some of the highest work-from-home shares in the country are here, in places with very few people. Perkins County, South Dakota, about one person per square mile, has a work-from-home share of 32.9%, sixth-highest of the 2,956 counties and above Fairfax County's 28.7%. Yet its inactivity rate, 23.6%, is unremarkable. Kidder County, North Dakota, is similar: 22.1% working from home, 24.1% inactive.

These numbers likely mean something different from home office work in a suburb. The data here can't say what Perkins County's home workers do, but Census Bureau research has long found self-employed workers overrepresented among home-based workers, and in the 1960s most were family farmers and professionals. The exercise question matters too. It asks about activity "other than your regular job." Someone who works hard all day outdoors can answer no. Across the 417 counties nationwide with fewer than six people per square mile, the correlation is −0.33, about half the national figure.

In the region, inactivity follows income far more closely than working from home. Within South Dakota, the correlation between median household income and inactivity is −0.78. The two South Dakota counties with the highest inactivity rates, Todd (42.3%) and Oglala Lakota (41.7%), have median household incomes near $42,000 and work-from-home shares under 4%.

Oglala Lakota County lies entirely within the Pine Ridge Reservation, and Todd County within the Rosebud Sioux Reservation. Their low incomes and poor health have a much stronger explanation than anything about work: generations of U.S. policy toward Native nations. The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 set the Black Hills apart for the Sioux; in 1877 Congress took them without the consent of three-fourths of adult men that the treaty required, a taking the Supreme Court ruled in 1980 must be paid for, with interest. In exchange for the "forced dispossession" of Native land and the removal of tribes from their homelands, the government promised services, but the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights found in 2018 that those programs "remain chronically underfunded": in 2016 the Indian Health Service spent $2,834 per person, against $9,990 per person in federal health spending nationwide.

It's older than the pandemic

If remote office work caused the pattern, you'd expect it to be weak before 2020. It wasn't. Using the 2015–2019 work-from-home shares, when the typical county had 4.5% of workers at home (against 8.7% in 2020–2024), the correlation with the 2023 inactivity estimates is already −0.51. With 2010–2014 shares it's −0.49. The places where people work from home have long been different kinds of places.

Income, education and a model

Several other county measures line up with inactivity at least as strongly as working from home does, and they line up with working from home, too.

body.title: What else lines up with skipping exercise
body.caption: Income per person, household income and the bachelor's degree share each line up with inactivity more closely than working from home does, and each rises with working from home too. Population density and median age barely line up with inactivity.

body.html:
When we hold income and education equal, comparing counties that rank alike on median household income and the bachelor's degree share, the link between working from home and inactivity shrinks from −0.62 to −0.22. Adding population density and median age brings it to −0.16. Within groups of counties at similar income levels it is between −0.36 and −0.56. Something is left, but most of the pattern is about who lives in a county, not how they get to work.

Age is a small factor partly by design: the inactivity rates are age-adjusted, so a county with many retirees is not marked down for it.

There's one more reason to be careful. The inactivity numbers aren't a direct count. CDC's PLACES project estimates them with a statistical model: it takes national survey answers and predicts each county's rate using its residents' age, sex, race and ethnicity, and education, plus the share of the county's adults living below 150% of the poverty line, from the same Census survey that measures working from home (CDC PLACES methodology). So education and poverty are two of the model's inputs, and they are also two of the strongest companions of working from home. Part of the correlation is built in by the way the estimates are made. That does not make the pattern false, but the county estimates may line up with education and poverty more neatly than the true rates do.

One more thing we couldn't test: the mix of jobs. Some jobs can be done from home and many can't. If the ones that can are concentrated in the same counties as college graduates and higher incomes, that alone would produce much of this pattern. Mapwich doesn't have county occupation data yet, so we can't separate the job from the person doing it.

What the map can't tell us

None of this shows that working from home makes anyone more active, or less. A correlation across counties is a statement about places, not people. The home workers in Arlington and the non-exercisers in Grayson County may not be the same people at all. Answering the real question would take data that follows individuals: how they work, and how they spend the time they don't spend commuting.

What the map does show is useful on its own. Places where working from home is common tend to be places where more adults stay active, and both tend to be places with more money and more college degrees. Where that bundle comes apart, as on the northern Plains, the work-from-home number stops predicting much at all.
